Complex vectors work mostly the same as real vectors (we can add them, multiply them by a scalar, etc). However, complex vectors have a few extra properties:

[MATH: [− 1 + \textrm{i}; 3 + 2\textrm{i}]]
- Complex vectors have a real and imaginary part. This means that we can write a vector in the form [MATH: \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{\color{blue}a} + \textrm{i}\mathbf{\color{red}b},] where [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}} = {\color{blue}\textrm{Re}(\mathbf{x})}] and [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{b}} = {\color{red}\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{x})}.]

Content:
The real part of the vector contains the real part of each entry, and the imaginary part of the vector contains the imaginary part of each entry:
[MATH: [− 1 + \textrm{i}; 3 + 2\textrm{i}]]

Since [MATH: \overline{k\mathbf{v}} = \overline{k} \, \overline{\mathbf{v}},] we get the following equation:

[MATH: kv^(―)|= k^(―)v^(―); [8\textrm{i} − 12; 0]|= k^(―)[− 4\textrm{i}; 0]^(―); [8\textrm{i} − 12; 0]|= k^(―)[− 4\textrm{i}^(―); 0^(―)]; [8\textrm{i} − 12; 0]|= k^(―)[4\textrm{i}; 0]; [8\textrm{i} − 12; 0]|= [4\textrm{i}k^(―); 0]]

So, we obtain that [MATH: 4\textrm{i}\,\overline{k} = 8\textrm{i}-12 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \overline{k}=\dfrac{8\textrm{i}-12}{4\textrm i} = 2+3\textrm{i}.]

Therefore, [MATH: k=\overline{2+3\textrm{i}}=2-3\textrm{i}.]

Finally, [MATH: \textrm{Im}(k)=-3.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Complex vectors are vectors whose entries are complex numbers, such as [MATH: [− 1 + \textrm{i}; 3 + 2\textrm{i}]] In general, [MATH: \mathbb{C}^n] is the space of complex vectors with [MATH: n] entries.

Content:
Complex vectors work mostly the same as real vectors (we can add them, multiply them by a scalar, etc). However, complex vectors have a few extra properties:

Content:
- We can take the complex conjugate of a vector by taking the complex conjugate of each component:
[MATH: [− 1 + \textrm{i}; 3 + 2\textrm{i}]]
- Complex vectors have a real and imaginary part. This means that we can write a vector in the form [MATH: \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{\color{blue}a} + \textrm{i}\mathbf{\color{red}b},] where [MATH: {\color{blue}\mathbf{a}} = {\color{blue}\textrm{Re}(\mathbf{x})}] and [MATH: {\color{red}\mathbf{b}} = {\color{red}\textrm{Im}(\mathbf{x})}.]

Content:
The real part of the vector contains the real part of each entry, and the imaginary part of the vector contains the imaginary part of each entry:
[MATH: [− 1 + \textrm{i}; 3 + 2\textrm{i}]]

---

Item 2 — Example: Calculating the Complex Conjugate of a Complex Vector

To find the complex conjugate of a vector, we take the complex conjugate of the entries of the vector. So, we have
[MATH: x^(―)|= [− 2 + 5\textrm{i}; 5 − 9\textrm{i}; − 7 + 8\textrm{i}]^(―); = [− 2 + 5\textrm{i}^(―); 5 − 9\textrm{i}^(―); − 7 + 8\textrm{i}^(―)]; = [− 2 − 5\textrm{i}; 5 + 9\textrm{i}; − 7 − 8\textrm{i}].]
